{{Short description|Probabilistic Condorcet method}}
{{Electoral systems}}

'''Maximal lotteries''' are a [[fractional social choice|probabilistic voting rule]] that use [[preferential ballot|ranked ballot]]s and returns a [[lottery (decision theory)|lottery]] over candidates that a majority of voters will prefer, in expectation, to any other. More formally, the rule has the property that, when averaging over a series of repeated head-to-head matchups, at least half of all voters will prefer the result of a maximal lottery to the result produced by any other [[voting rule]].<ref name="Fish84a">{{Cite journal|title=Probabilistic Social Choice Based on Simple Voting Comparisons|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2297786|journal=The Review of Economic Studies|date=1984|issn=0034-6527|pages=683–692|volume=51|issue=4|doi=10.2307/2297786|first=P. C.|last=Fishburn}}</ref>

Maximal lotteries satisfy a wide range of desirable properties: they elect the [[Condorcet winner criterion|Condorcet winner]] with probability 1 if it exists<ref name="Fish84a" /> and never elect candidates outside the [[Smith criterion|Smith set]].<ref name="Fish84a" /> Moreover, they satisfy [[independence of clones]].<ref name="Bran13a" /> The probabilistic voting rule that returns all maximal lotteries is the only rule satisfying reinforcement, Condorcet-consistency, and independence of clones.<ref name="Bran13a" /> The [[social welfare function]] that top-ranks maximal lotteries has been uniquely characterized using Arrow's [[independence of irrelevant alternatives]] and [[Pareto efficiency]].<ref name="BrBr19a">F. Brandl and F. Brandt. [http://dss.in.tum.de/files/brandt-research/welfare.pdf Arrovian Aggregation of Convex Preferences]. Econometrica. 88(2), pages 799-844, 2020.</ref>

Maximal lotteries do not satisfy the standard notion of strategyproofness, as [[Allan Gibbard]] has shown that only [[dictatorship mechanism|random dictatorships]] can satisfy strategyproofness and ex post efficiency.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gibbard|first=Allan|date=1977|title=Manipulation of Schemes that Mix Voting with Chance|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1911681|journal=Econometrica|volume=45|issue=3|pages=665–681|doi=10.2307/1911681|jstor=1911681|issn=0012-9682|hdl=10419/220534|hdl-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Maximal lotteries are also [[Monotonicity criterion|nonmonotonic]] in probabilities, meaning it is possible for the probability of an alternative to decrease if  this alternative up.<ref name="Fish84a"/> However, they satisfy relative monotonicity, the probability of <math>x</math> relative to that of <math>y</math> does not decrease when <math>x</math> is improved over <math>y</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brandl |first=Florian |last2=Brandt |first2=Felix |last3=Stricker |first3=Christian |date=2022-01-01 |title=An analytical and experimental comparison of maximal lottery schemes |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00355-021-01326-x |journal=Social Choice and Welfare |language=en |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=5–38 |doi=10.1007/s00355-021-01326-x |issn=1432-217X|hdl=10419/286729 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 

The maximal lottery satisfies some generalizations of [[Consistency criterion|reinforcement]]<ref name="Bran13a">F. Brandl, F. Brandt, and H. G. Seedig. [https://dss.in.tum.de/files/brandt-research/conlott.pdf Consistent probabilistic social choice]. Econometrica. 84(5), pages 1839-1880, 2016.</ref> and [[Participation criterion|participation]]<ref name="Bran15a">F. Brandl, F. Brandt, and J. Hofbauer. [https://dss.in.tum.de/files/brandt-research/mlpart.pdf Welfare Maximization Entices Participation]. Games and Economic Behavior. 14, pages 308-314, 2019.</ref> to the non-deterministic case: the [[probability of superiority]] exceeds 50%, meaning a voter will prefer the result they get by participating to the one they get by not participating more than half the time.<ref name="Bran15a" /> However, a maximal lottery can still exhibit a no-show paradox in the [[expected utility]] sense, so a voter feels the lottery they get by voting is worse (has lower expected utility) than the lottery they would receive if they had not turned out.

The [[Support (mathematics)|support]] of maximal lotteries, which is known as the ''essential set'' or the ''{{vanchor|bipartisan set}}'', has been studied in detail.<ref name="DL99">B. Dutta and J.-F. Laslier. ''Comparison functions and choice correspondences''. Social Choice and Welfare, 16: 513–532, 1999.</ref><ref name="LLL93b">G. Laffond, J.-F. Laslier, and M. Le Breton. ''The bipartisan set of a tournament game''. Games and Economic Behavior, 5(1):182–201, 1993.</ref><ref name="Laslier97">[[:fr:Jean-François Laslier|Laslier, J.-F.]] ''Tournament solutions and majority voting'' Springer-Verlag, 1997.</ref><ref name="BBHS18">{{Cite journal|title=On the structure of stable tournament solutions|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00199-016-1024-x|journal=Economic Theory|date=2018-03-01|issn=0938-2259|pages=483–507|volume=65|issue=2|doi=10.1007/s00199-016-1024-x|language=en|first=Felix|last=Brandt|first2=Markus|last2=Brill|first3=Hans Georg|last3=Seedig|first4=Warut|last4=Suksompong|arxiv=2004.01651}}</ref>

== History ==
Maximal lotteries were first proposed by the French mathematician and social scientist Germain Kreweras in 1965<ref name="Krew65a">G. Kreweras. ''Aggregation of preference orderings''. In Mathematics and Social Sciences I: Proceedings of the seminars of Menthon-Saint-Bernard, France (1–27 July 1960) and of Gösing, Austria (3–27 July 1962), pages 73–79, 1965.</ref> and popularized by [[Peter C. Fishburn|Peter Fishburn]].<ref name="Fish84a" /> Since then, they have been rediscovered multiple times by economists,<ref name="LLL93b" /> mathematicians,<ref name="Fish84a" /><ref name="FiRy95a">{{Cite journal|title=Tournament games and positive tournaments|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jgt.3190190208|journal=Journal of Graph Theory|date=1995|issn=1097-0118|pages=217–236|volume=19|issue=2|doi=10.1002/jgt.3190190208|language=en|first=David C.|last=Fisher|first2=Jennifer|last2=Ryan|url-access=subscription}}</ref> political scientists, philosophers,<ref name="FeMa92a">{{Cite journal|title=After two centuries, should condorcet's voting procedure be implemented?|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/bs.3830370403|journal=Behavioral Science|date=1992|issn=1099-1743|pages=250–274|volume=37|issue=4|doi=10.1002/bs.3830370403|language=en|first=Dan S.|last=Felsenthal|first2=Moshé|last2=Machover|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and computer scientists.<ref name="RiSh10a">[[Ron Rivest|R. L. Rivest]] and E. Shen. ''An optimal single-winner preferential voting system based on game theory''. In Proceedings of 3rd International Workshop on Computational Social Choice, pages 399–410, 2010.</ref>

Several natural dynamics that converge to maximal lotteries have been observed in biology, physics, chemistry, and machine learning.<ref name="LL17">{{Cite journal|title=Reinforcement learning from comparisons: Three alternatives are enough, two are not|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-applied-probability/volume-27/issue-5/Reinforcement-learning-from-comparisons--Three-alternatives-are-enough-two/10.1214/16-AAP1271.full|journal=The Annals of Applied Probability|date=2017-10-01|issn=1050-5164|volume=27|issue=5|doi=10.1214/16-AAP1271|first=Benoît|last=Laslier|first2=Jean-François|last2=Laslier|pages=2907–2925}}</ref><ref name="Grillil17">{{Cite journal|title=Higher-order interactions stabilize dynamics in competitive network models|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature23273|journal=Nature|date=2017-08-01|issn=1476-4687|pages=210–213|volume=548|issue=7666|doi=10.1038/nature23273|language=en|first=Jacopo|last=Grilli|first2=György|last2=Barabás|first3=Matthew J.|last3=Michalska-Smith|first4=Stefano|last4=Allesina|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="BrBr21a">F. Brandl and F. Brandt. [https://pub.dss.in.tum.de/brandt-research/dynamic_ml.pdf A Natural Adaptive Process for Collective Decision-Making]. Theoretical Economics 19(2): 667–703, 2024.</ref>

== Collective preferences over lotteries ==

The input to this voting system consists of the agents' ordinal preferences over outcomes (not lotteries over alternatives), but a relation on the set of lotteries can be constructed in the following way: if <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are lotteries over alternatives, <math>p\succ q</math> if the expected value of the margin of victory of an outcome selected with distribution <math>p</math> in a head-to-head vote against an outcome selected with distribution <math>q</math> is positive. In other words, <math>p\succ q</math> if it is more likely that a randomly selected voter will prefer the alternatives sampled from <math>p</math> to the alternative sampled from <math>q</math> than vice versa.<ref name=BrBr19a /> While this relation is not necessarily transitive, it does always admit at least one maximal element.

It is possible that several such maximal lotteries exist, as a result of ties. However, the maximal lottery is unique whenever the number of voters is odd.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=A Theorem on Symmetric Two-Player Zero-Sum Games|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022053196922152|journal=Journal of Economic Theory|date=1997-02-01|issn=0022-0531|pages=426–431|volume=72|issue=2|doi=10.1006/jeth.1996.2215|first=Gilbert|last=Laffond|first2=Jean-Francois|last2=Laslier|first3=Michel|last3=Le Breton|url-access=subscription}}</ref> By the same argument, the bipartisan set is uniquely defined by taking the support of the unique maximal lottery that solves a tournament game.<ref name="LLL93b"/>

== Strategic interpretation ==

Maximal lotteries are equivalent to mixed [[Minimax|maximin strategies]] (or [[Nash equilibria]]) of the symmetric [[zero-sum game]] given by the pairwise majority margins. As such, they have a natural interpretation in terms of electoral competition between two political parties<ref name="Laslier2000">[[:fr:Jean-François Laslier|Laslier, J.-F.]] ''Interpretation of electoral mixed strategies''. Social Choice and Welfare 17: pages 283–292, 2000.</ref> and can be computed in polynomial time via linear programming.

== Example ==
Suppose there are five voters who have the following preferences over three alternatives:
* 2 voters: <math>a\succ b\succ c</math>
* 2 voters: <math>b\succ c\succ a</math>
* 1 voter: <math>c\succ a\succ b</math>

The pairwise preferences of the voters can be represented in the following [[skew-symmetric matrix]], where the entry for row <math>x</math> and column <math>y</math> denotes the number of voters who prefer <math>x</math> to <math>y</math> minus the number of voters who prefer <math>y</math> to <math>x</math>.

<math>
\begin{matrix}
 \begin{matrix}
  &  & a\quad & b\quad & c\quad \\
 \end{matrix}
 \\
 \begin{matrix}
  a\\
  b\\
  c\\
 \end{matrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}
  0 & 1 & -1\\
  -1 & 0 & 3\\
  1 & -3 & 0\\  
 \end{pmatrix}
\end{matrix}</math>

This matrix can be interpreted as a [[zero-sum game]] and admits a unique [[Nash equilibrium]] (or [[minimax strategy]]) <math>p</math> where <math>p(a)=3/5</math>, <math>p(b)=1/5</math>, <math>p(c)=1/5</math>. By definition, this is also the unique maximal lottery of the preference profile above. The example was carefully chosen not to have a [[Condorcet winner]]. Many preference profiles admit a Condorcet winner, in which case the unique maximal lottery will assign probability 1 to the Condorcet winner. If the last voter in the example above swaps alternatives <math>a</math> and <math>c</math> in his preference relation, <math>a</math> becomes the Condorcet winner and will be selected with probability 1.
